"Alif-Lãm-Mĩm" The chapter opens with three letters of the Arabic alphabet, and the Jalālayn reads them as letters whose meaning God knows best. The Mukhtaṣar explains the same point, that the inability of the Arabs to produce a Qurʾān like this is the sign of its divine origin. The Tanwīr reads the letters as a mark of the miracle that the Qurʾān carries. The Qushayrī commentary reads the letters as an allusion to the sufficiency of God for His servant. The Tazkirul commentary states that man has always put many different constructions upon the teachings of God, and that the Qurʾān is a genuine book of guidance. The reader is asked to see the opening letters as a call to the heart before the reading begins, and to see the Qurʾān as the book of guidance that stands above all the constructions that men have placed upon it.

2.text:
"Allah! There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him—the Ever-Living, All-Sustaining" The verse opens with the name of Allah and with the declaration that there is no god but Him. The Jalālayn reads the verse as the statement that there is no god except Him, the Living, the Eternal. The Maʿārif commentary takes the words there is no god but He as the central statement of the oneness of God, and it treats the absolute denial of any other god as its full meaning. The Ibn Kathīr commentary reads the Ever-Living as the one who does not die, and the All-Sustaining as the one who maintains all things. The Mukhtaṣar explains that Allah alone deserves to be worshipped, and that He is the one who lives perfectly without any death or deficiency. The Tanwīr reads the Alive as the one who dies not, and the Qushayrī commentary reads the verse as the statement that God is not too busy to attend to His servants. The reader is asked to see the verse as the foundation on which the rest of the chapter stands, since every argument that follows rests on this declaration of the oneness and the life of Allah.

**The oneness of Allah.**

In the words (Allah: there is no god but He) which follow immediately, the doctrine of the Oneness of Allah has been put forth as a categorical declaration.

**Worthy of worship.**

It means that there is absolutely nothing worthy of worship other than Allah. (Allah! None has the right to be worshipped but He, the Ever Living, the One Who sustains and protects all that exists) and,.

**Living and Eternal.**

(Allah! There is no God save Him, the Alive) Who dies not and is not evanescent, (the Eternal) the Self-subsistent Who has no beginning. Allah is the One Who alone deserves to be worshipped.

**Maintaining all things.**

But man has always put different constructions upon divine teachings.

**What else the same passage holds.**

The first verse of this section presents a rational proof of the Oneness of Allah; the second verse, the reported proof 1, followed by an answer to some doubts nursed by disbelievers towards the later part. There is no god except Him the Living the Eternal. In the terminology of Islamic theology, a proof based on rational argument is called rational proof while a proof based on a verse of divine book or on a declaration made by an authority or a report narrated by a trustworthy person is called a reported proof. The first word, Alif Lam Mim at the head of the first verse be-longs to the special set of words used by the Qur'an which are words of hidden meaning and are known as Mutashabihat the real meaning of which is a secret between Allah and His Messenger and the details of which appear a little later in the section. Then come the words (the Alive, the All-Sustaining) which lay out a rational proof of the Oneness of Allah. The essence of the argument is that worship means to present oneself before somebody in utter submission and humility. It, therefore, requires that the one who is being worshipped must occupy the highest point of honour and power and who has to be most perfect from all angles. From this it is obvious that anything which cannot sustain its own being, rather is dependent upon somebody else for its very existence, could hardly claim to have any honour or power in its own right.

For example, the Holy Qur'an has clarified the position of Sayyidna Isa (Jesus Christ) by saying (he is nothing but a servant upon whom We have bestowed Our blessing 43:59), or as elsewhere in the Qur'an, by ‌ (the example of Isa before Allah is like that of Adam whom He created from clay - 3:59). These and several other verses like them show it clearly that Sayyidn Isa Masih, is a chosen servant of Allah created by Him. Therefore, the claim of Christians investing him with godhood and son ship is not correct. Now, if someone closes his eyes towards all these verses which have an established meaning and unnecessarily coils with the expressions, (the Word of Allah) and ‌ (a spirit from Him) and their likes from the category of Mutashabihat (verses whose definite meanings cannot be ascertained) and starts deducing from them meanings which are against the Muhkamat of Qur'an and other consistent statements, then, that would be a simple case of going astray and being ob-stinate.

8.text:
"˹They say,˺ “Our Lord! Do not let our hearts deviate after you have guided us. Grant us Your mercy. You are indeed the Giver ˹of all bounties˺" The verse gives the prayer of those who are well grounded in knowledge, who ask their Lord to keep their hearts steady after the guidance has come. The Jalālayn reads the prayer as the request that the Lord not cause the hearts to incline toward falsehood. The Maʿārif commentary explains that these people chose to have faith in what comes from their Lord, and that they ask Him to keep them on the path. The Ibn Kathīr commentary reads the mercy as the grace that the believers ask from Allah to keep their hearts firm. The Tanwīr reads the Giver as the one who bestows every good upon the believer, and the Mukhtaṣar explains that Allah is the one who saves from what befell those who moved away from the truth. The Tazkirul commentary states that one should be content with an abstract understanding of the things that are beyond the senses, and that the believer must accept what he cannot fully see. The Qushayrī commentary reads the prayer as a plea for a bounty that is not repaid by any deed, but given by mercy alone. The reader is asked to see the verse as the prayer of the firm in knowledge, who fear the turning of the heart and seek the mercy of their Lord to keep it steady.

**Our hearts do not deviate.**

Our Lord do not cause our hearts to deviate do not cause them to incline away from the truth in their desire to interpret it such as is inappropriate for us — as You caused the hearts of those others to deviate — after You have guided us after You have shown us the way to it; and give us mercy from You as a strengthening; You are the Bestower. Instead of that, they elected to have faith in what comes from their Lord.

**Grant us Your mercy.**

(they follow that which is not entirely clear thereof) meaning, they refer to the Mutashabih, because they are able to alter its meanings to conform with their false interpretation since the wordings of the Mutashabihat encompass such a wide area of meanings. One should be content to have an abstract understanding of the things which cannot be grasped precisely by the senses.

**The Giver of all bounties.**

(Lo! Thou, only Thou art the Bestower) to the believers before us; it is also said that this means: Save us from what happened to those who moved away from the truth.

**Content with what the senses miss.**

And give what you give, O Lord, as Your bounty and mercy, not as the recompense for our works or the compensation for our acts of obedience! (Cause not our hearts to stray) do not make our hearts deviate from Your Religion (after Thou hast guided us) to Your Religion, (and bestow upon us mercy from Thy Presence) make us firm in holding to Your religion.

**What else the same passage holds.**

In it are verses that are entirely clear, they are the foundations of the Book; and others not entirely clear. So as for those in whose hearts there is a deviation (from the truth) they follow (only) that which is not entirely clear thereof, seeking Al-Fitnah, and seeking its Ta'wil, but none knows its Ta'wil except Allah. The previous verse mentioned 'those well-grounded in knowledge' who, in spite of their excellent knowledge, were not proud of their excellence. The present verse mentions yet another excellence of theirs - that they pray for steadfastness on the right path, not for any worldly gains, but for salvation in the life-to-come. The first verse shows us that guidance and straying are from Allah alone. When Allah intends to guide someone, He makes his heart tilt towards what is good and right; and when He decides to let someone go astray, He turns his heart away from the straight path. This is just as it was said in a hadith of the Holy Prophet There is no heart which is not there in between the two of Allah's fingers - He makes it firm on the truth as long as He wills, and turns it away from the truth when He wills. Therefore, those who are concerned about how to remain firm in their faith, they go to the source - requesting and praying Allah for steadfastness. The Holy Prophet always used to pray for it as it appears in a hadith: ( O reverser of hearts, make our hearts firm on the faith chosen by You).

9.text:
"Our Lord! You will certainly gather all humanity for the ˹promised˺ Day—about which there is no doubt. Surely Allah does not break His promise.”" The verse turns to the Day of Gathering, which the believers ask their Lord to bring about in the proper time. The Ibn Kathīr commentary gives the sense that Allah keeps His promise, and that the Day is sure to come as He has promised. The Tanwīr reads the gathering as the act of Allah, who brings people together after they die. The Tazkirul commentary states that man turns away from the truth in order to safeguard his worldly interests, and that the Day of Gathering is the answer to this. The Qushayrī commentary reads the Day as the gathering of the lovers of God in the presence of their Lord. The reader is asked to see the verse as the close of the prayer of the firm in knowledge, who look to the certain Day as the place where the promise of their Lord is kept. The reader is asked to see the verse as the place where the prayer for the Day is joined to the certainty of the promise, so that the believer waits for the Day with hope and with trust in the word of his Lord.

**The gathering of mankind.**

Our Lord You shall gather mankind for a day that is on a day of which there is no doubt no uncertainty that is the Day of Resurrection when You will requite them for their deeds as You had promised; verily God will not fail the tryst His promise of the Upraising there is a shift of address here from the second to the third person and these last words could constitute God’s speech. So as for those in whose hearts there is a deviation (from the truth) they follow (only) that which is not entirely clear thereof, seeking Al-Fitnah, and seeking its Ta'wil, but none knows its Ta'wil except Allah. (it is Thou Who gatherest mankind together) after they die (to a Day) on a day (of which there is no doubt. Lo! Today is the gathering of the lovers on the carpet of approach iqtirāb and tomorrow will be the gathering of all in the place of reward thawāb and punishment ʿiqāb. That is why, in order to safeguard his interests, man turns away from the truth.

The purpose of their supplication in this way is to show that their concern is with the matter of the Hereafter and for this reason they ask God for adherence to the path of guidance in order to attain its reward. In it are verses that are entirely clear, they are the foundations of the Book; and others not entirely clear. The two Shaykhs Bukhārī and Muslim reported that ‘Ā’isha may God be pleased with her said ‘The Messenger of God s recited this verse It is He Who revealed to you the Book wherein are verses clear to the end of the verse and said “When you see those pursuing the allegorical parts know that these are the ones God refers to in this verse so beware of them” ’. This is just as it was said in a hadith of the Holy Prophet There is no heart which is not there in between the two of Allah's fingers - He makes it firm on the truth as long as He wills, and turns it away from the truth when He wills. 10.text:
"Indeed, neither the wealth nor children of the disbelievers will be of any benefit to them against Allah, and they will be the fuel for the Fire" The verse states neither the wealth nor the children of the disbelievers will benefit them before Allah, and that they will be the fuel of the Fire. The Jalālayn reads the sentence as the statement that neither riches nor children will avail the disbelievers against Allah. The Maʿārif commentary takes the text as moving from the verbal confrontation with the disbelievers to the warning of what their possessions will not do for them. The Ibn Kathīr commentary states that Allah makes clear that the disbelievers to be the fuel for the Fire. The Tazkirul commentary explains that man turns away from the truth to safeguard his worldly interests, and that he is not ready to give up his friends and relatives for the sake of the truth. The Tanwīr reads the riches and the progeny as the wealth of the disbelievers on that Day, and it gives the example of Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf and his companions. The Mukhtaṣar explains that the wealth and children of the disbelievers in Allah and His Messenger will not save them from the punishment. The Qushayrī commentary reads the verse as the statement that the possessions of this world will not be a shield on the Day of Return. The reader is asked to see the verse as the place where the goods that the disbeliever trusts are shown to be empty before the Lord.

**Riches and children.**

As for the disbelievers neither their riches nor their children will avail will protect them against God that is against His chastisement; those — they shall be fuel for the Fire they shall constitute what the Fire will be fuelled by read waqūd as opposed to wuqūd ‘fuel’. The text now shifts from the verbal confrontation with disbelievers on the warnings about the coming physical encounter as pointed out in verse 12 - 'You shall soon be overcome (by Muslims) ' while the verses earlier (10 and 11) serve as the introduction.

**Fuel for the Fire.**

If it means abandoning his friends and relatives, he is not ready to join a lone preacher (da‘i).

**The example of Kaʿb.**

Ka'b Ibn al-Ashraf and his fellow companions; and it is also said that this refers to Abu Jahl and his companions (will aught avail them with Allah) will not avail them anything from Allah's torment. Such disbelievers will be the fuel with which Hell will be lit on the Day of Resurrection.

**Possessions on the Day of Return.**

He is saying, "Tomorrow at the res urrection possessions and children will be useless to the unbelievers and will not profit them.

**What else the same passage holds.**

Verily, those who disbelieve, neither their properties nor their offspring will avail them whatsoever against Allah; and it is they who will be fuel of the Fire Like the behavior of the people of Fir'awn and those before them; they belied Our Ayat. On the Day of Resurrection, No Wealth or Offspring Shall Avail Allah states that the disbelievers shall be fuel for the Fire, Further, what they were granted in this life of wealth and offspring shall not avail them with Allah, or save them from His punishment and severe torment. (So let not their wealth nor their children amaze you; in reality Allah's plan is to punish them with these things in the life of this world, and that their souls shall depart while they are disbelievers.)[9:55], and, (Verily, those who disbelieve) meaning, disbelieved in Allah's Ayat, denied His Messengers, defied His Books and did not benefit from His revelation to His Prophets, (Neither their properties nor their offspring will avail them whatsoever against Allah; and it is they who will be fuel of the Fire.) meaning, they will be the wood with which the Fire is kindled and fed. (Like the Da'b of the people of Fira'wn.) Ad-Dahhak said that Ibn 'Abbas said that the Ayah means, "Like the behavior of the people of Fir'awn. " This is the same Tafsir of 'Ikrimah, Mujahid, Abu Malik, Ad-Dahhak, and others. Other scholars said that the Ayah means, "Like the practice, conduct, likeness of the people of Fir'awn. " These meanings are all plausible, for the Da'b means practice, behavior, tradition and habit. The Ayah indicates that the disbelievers will not benefit from their wealth or offspring.

11.text:
"Their fate will be like that of the people of Pharaoh and those before them, they all rejected Our signs, so Allah seized them for their sins. And Allah is severe in punishment" The verse compares the case of these disbelievers with the people of Pharaoh and those who came before them. The Jalālayn reads the way of these people as the habit of the folk of Pharaoh and of the communities that went before. The Maʿārif commentary takes the text as the continuation of the same warning, and it places the wealth and children of the disbelievers beside the fate of the earlier nations. Their way is as the way as the habit of Pharaoh’s folk and the communities of people before them such as ‘Ād and Thamūd who denied Our signs; God seized them He destroyed them for their sins this statement explains the previous one; God is severe in retribution. Further, what they were granted in this life of wealth and offspring shall not avail them with Allah, or save them from His punishment and severe torment. But all the material considerations that appear important today will cease to matter on the Day of Judgement.

The Day the veil of Doomsday is rent asunder, and all issues are to be settled between man and God, all worldly things will become insignificant—as if they had never existed. The missionary in this world appears to be powerless, but in reality, he is powerful, because God is backing him. The denier appears to be influential in this world, but is, in fact, totally powerless, because his strength is nothing but a temporary delusion. On the Day of Resurrection, No Wealth or Offspring Shall Avail Allah states that the disbelievers shall be fuel for the Fire, (So let not their wealth nor their children amaze you; in reality Allah's plan is to punish them with these things in the life of this world, and that their souls shall depart while they are disbelievers.)[9:55], and, (Verily, those who disbelieve) meaning, disbelieved in Allah's Ayat, denied His Messengers, defied His Books and did not benefit from His revelation to His Prophets, (Neither their properties nor their offspring will avail them whatsoever against Allah; and it is they who will be fuel of the Fire.) meaning, they will be the wood with which the Fire is kindled and fed. (Like the Da'b of the people of Fira'wn.) Ad-Dahhak said that Ibn 'Abbas said that the Ayah means, "Like the behavior of the people of Fir'awn. " This is the same Tafsir of 'Ikrimah, Mujahid, Abu Malik, Ad-Dahhak, and others. Other scholars said that the Ayah means, "Like the practice, conduct, likeness of the people of Fir'awn. " These meanings are all plausible, for the Da'b means practice, behavior, tradition and habit. The Ayah indicates that the disbelievers will not benefit from their wealth or offspring. This is the same end the people of Fir'awn and the previous nations met, those who rejected the Messengers, the Ayat, and proofs of Allah that they were sent with. (And Allah is severe in punishment.) meaning, His punishment is severe and His torment is painful. None can escape Allah's grasp, nor does anything escape His knowledge. Allah does what He wills and prevails over all things, it is He to Whom everything is humbled and there is no deity worthy of worship, nor any Lord except Him.

12.text:
"O Prophet! Tell the disbelievers, “Soon you will be overpowered and driven to Hell, what an evil place to rest!”" The verse is addressed to the Prophet, who is told to say to the disbelievers that they will soon be overpowered and driven to Hell. The Jalālayn reads the instruction as the command to proclaim the warning to the disbelievers, and it places the verse in the period when the Jews were called to enter Islam. The Maʿārif commentary explains that the disbelievers referred to here are the ones who had been defeated, and it explains that the doubt of some readers about the verse is without ground. The Ibn Kathīr commentary gives the words of the warning as the sign that the disbelievers will be gathered together to Hell, and it states that Allah commanded the Prophet to proclaim this to them. The Tazkirul commentary reads the verse against the background of the worldly comfort that the disbelievers held dear. The Tanwīr gives the sense of the unbelievers of Makkah as the people addressed, and it reads the overpowering as the defeat that was to come at the Day of Badr. The Mukhtaṣar explains that Allah will gather the disbelievers in the fire of Hell. The Qushayrī commentary reads the verse as the statement that the speech of the Real will not reach them in the Fire. The reader is asked to see the verse as a warning given with certainty, and as a promise that the defeat of the disbelievers will be made plain.

**Soon you will be overpowered.**

When the Prophet s enjoined the Jews to enter into Islam after his return from Badr they said ‘Do not fool yourself just because you killed a few men of Quraysh inexperienced and knowing nothing about fighting’ whereupon the following was revealed Say O Muhammad to the disbelievers from among the Jews ‘You shall be vanquished sa-tughlabūn or read sa-yughlabūn ‘they shall be vanquished’ in this world through being killed or taken captive and made to pay the jizya which actually took place and mustered read in both ways wa-tuhsharūna ‘you will be mustered’ or wa-yuhsharūna ‘they will be mustered’ in the Hereafter to Hell which you shall enter — an evil cradling!’ an evil resting place. But, this doubt is unfounded as the disbelievers referred to here are the disbelievers and Jews of that particular time - from among whom, the pagans were overcome when killed or taken prisoners, and the Jews were overcome through killing or imprisonment as well as through Jizya and extradition.

**Driven to Hell.**

Allah commanded the Prophet Muhammad to proclaim to the disbelievers,. On the one hand, there are all the assets of worldly comfort and grandeur, while, on the other hand, there is the caravan of truth, having no foothold in society, and no worldly interests attached to it.

**The day of Badr.**

(Ye shall be overcome) You shall be killed on the Day of Badr (and gathered unto hell) on the Day of Judgement, (an evil resting place) an evil place and outcome. Allah will then gather you in the fire of Hell.

**What an evil place to rest.**

He informed them that the speech of the Real will elude them in the future ājil and they will have no delight in living in the present #703;ājil. Allah commanded the Prophet Muhammad to proclaim to the disbelievers,.

**What else the same passage holds.**

When the call of Truth goes out, it appears to people to be of no value. "You will be defeated and gathered together to Hell, and worst indeed is that place of rest. There has already been a sign for you in the two armies that met. In such a situation, joining the caravan of truth amounts to detachment from the social circle and depriving oneself of all material benefits. One was fighting in the cause of Allah, and as for the other, in disbelief. That is why, in order to safeguard his interests, man turns away from the truth. They saw them with their own eyes twice their number. If it means abandoning his friends and relatives, he is not ready to join a lone preacher (da‘i). And Allah supports with His aid whom He wills. Verily, in this is a lesson for those who understand Some readers of verse 12: ‌ just cited, above may have some doubt about disbelievers being overcome because this is not the case with all disbelievers of the world. Threatening the Jews With Defeat and Encouraging Them to Learn a Lesson From the Battle of Badr Therefore, this 'overcoming' of disbelievers mentioned in the verse simply does not refer to disbelievers universally. (And gathered together) on the Day of Resurrection, Muhammad bin Ishaq bin Yasar recorded that 'Asim bin 'Umar bin Qatadah said that when the Messenger of Allah gained victory in the battle of Badr and went back to Al-Madīnah, he gathered the Jews in the marketplace of Bani Qaynuqa'. (There has already been a sign for you) meaning, O Jews, who said what you said! You have an Ayah, meaning proof, that Allah will make His religion prevail, award victory to His Messenger, make His Word apparent and His religion the highest. (One was fighting in the Cause of Allah) the Muslims, (And as for the other, in disbelief) meaning, the idolators of Quraysh at Badr. It was said that the meaning of Allah's statement, When we looked at them again, we thought they did not have one man more than we had. (And (remember) when you met, He showed them to you as few in your eyes and He made you appear as few in their eyes.)[8:44]". When the two camps saw each other, the Muslims thought that the idolators were twice as many as they were, so that they would trust in Allah and seek His help. The idolators thought that the believers were twice as many as they were, so that they would feel fear, horror, fright and despair. When the two camps stood in lines and met in battle, Allah made each camp look smaller in the eyes of the other camp, so that they would be encouraged to fight each other, (so that Allah might accomplish a matter already ordained.)[8:42] meaning, so that the truth and falsehood are distinguishable, and thus the word of faith prevails over disbelief and deviation, so that the believers prevail and the disbelievers are humiliated. They should contemplate about Allah's wisdom, decisions and decree, that He gives victory to His believing servants in this life and on the Day the witnesses stand up to testify.

13.text:
"Indeed, there was a sign for you in the two armies that met in battle, one fighting for the cause of Allah and the other in denial. The believers saw their enemy twice their number. But Allah supports with His victory whoever He wills. Surely in this is a lesson for people of insight" The verse speaks of a sign that was given to the people in the two armies that met in battle. The Jalālayn reads the sign as a lesson for those with vision, and it explains that the example is the lesson drawn from the meeting of the two hosts. The Maʿārif commentary takes the verse as a reference to the Battle of Badr, in which the disbelievers had the greater number and the believers had the weaker force. The Ibn Kathīr commentary describes the one army as fighting in the cause of Allah, and the other as in disbelief. The Tazkirul commentary states that the believers were so few in number that they were powerless, and that those who denied the truth suffered a crushing defeat despite their numbers. The Tanwīr reads the sign as the confirmation of the prophethood of Muhammad, and it reads the army that fought in the way of Allah as the one that fought in obedience to Him. The Mukhtaṣar explains that there was a clear sign in the two groups that met to fight, and that one group was made up of believers. The Qushayrī commentary reads the verse as the lesson for the people of vision, who see past the numbers to the reality. The reader is asked to see the verse as the proof that the victory belongs to Allah and not to the number of the fighters.

**A sign in the two armies.**

Surely in that which is mentioned is a lesson for people of vision those who are discerning so will you not be warned by this and become believers? They had hopes of Allah's help, and ultimate victory, because they had placed their total trust in Allah, were steadfast and sincerely believed in the promise of Allah revealed to them in the following words:

**One army fighting for Allah.**

In fact, the believers were so few in number that they were powerless.

**The confirmation of prophethood.**

(one army fighting in the way of Allah) in obedience of Allah: One group was made up of believers, and this was the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions: they were fighting for Allah’s sake and in order to raise His Word against the word of those who disbelieve.

**A lesson for people of vision.**

**What else the same passage holds.**

There has already been a sign an example the verb qad kāna ‘there has been’ is used to separate the statement to follow from the previous one for you in two hosts two parties that met one another in battle on the day of Badr; one company fighting in the way of God in obedience to Him namely the Prophet and his Companions who numbered three hundred and thirteen men most of them on foot with two horses six plates of armour and eight swords; and another unbelieving; they the disbelievers numbering almost a thousand saw them the Muslims twice the like of them that is more numerous than themselves as the eye sees in manifest vision witnessing; and God granted them victory despite their fewer number; for God confirms He strengthens with His help whom He will granting him victory. The battle of Badr in the fourteenth year of the prophethood was a worldly example of what will happen in the next world. "You will be defeated and gathered together to Hell, and worst indeed is that place of rest. Those who deny the truth greatly exceeded the believers in numbers and in strength. There has already been a sign for you in the two armies that met. One was fighting in the cause of Allah, and as for the other, in disbelief. They saw them with their own eyes twice their number. And Allah supports with His aid whom He wills. Verily, in this is a lesson for those who understand In the previous verses, the disbelievers were informed that they will be overcome. Threatening the Jews With Defeat and Encouraging Them to Learn a Lesson From the Battle of Badr Now, cited in this verse is an example of how the prophecy has been fulfilled. Allah commanded the Prophet Muhammad to proclaim to the disbelievers, This verse refers to the Battle of Badr in which the disbelievers had about 1000 men, 700 camels and 100 horses, while the Muslim mujahidin were just over 300, having a total of 70 camels, 2 horses, 6 armours and 8 swords. The encounter was certainly strange as each combating group saw the opponent being twice its own numbers. The sighting of so many Muslims inspired awe in the hearts of the disbelievers, while Muslims who saw the disbelievers as twice of them turned to Allah more fervently. If there be among you a hundred patient one, they shall over-come two hundred. If the actual number of disbelievers which was three times more than their own were to be realized by Muslims, they may have been overawed. (And gathered together) on the Day of Resurrection, This state of sighting the numbers of the other group as twice its own was at a particular time. (One was fighting in the Cause of Allah) the Muslims, (And as for the other, in disbelief) meaning, the idolators of Quraysh at Badr. Beautified for mankind is love of lusts that which the self lusts after and calls for beautified by Satan or by God as a test — of women children stored-up heaps of gold and silver horses of mark fine horses cattle namely camels cows and sheep and tillage the cultivation of land. That the hostility of disbelievers should be countered with Jihad against them was the theme in several previous verses. Now, in these verses the text explains the reason why the disbelievers indulge in hostility against Islam and Muslims. There are all sorts of people who line up against the truth - some driven by greed for wealth or power, some goaded by lust and some in defence of false ancestral customs: All this is just to grab a share in the temporal enjoyments of the present life which has been described in these verses. The first verse here names some of the most de-sired things and says that they have been made to look attractive and therefore, people go after them enticed by their glamour brushing aside any concerns for the life to come, if there be any. For whatever man goes about procuring is because of the needs of his family - wife and children - to share it with him. Then come other forms of wealth and possessions - gold, silver, cattle and tillage - which attract people secondarily. Why has man been made in a way that he is temperamentally attracted to these things? The answer is that Allah has done so in His ultimate wisdom. If man was not naturally inclined to and even enamoured with these things, all worldly business would have gone topsy-turvy. Why would a wage-earner or an entrepreneur burn themselves out in an industry, or a business-man would put his capital and labour in buying and selling things? The secret was that the people of the world were made to grow and survive through this instinctive love for such things whereby they would go about collecting and preserving these. The well-to-do goes out to hire a worker for his job. The trader brings forth his best merchandise for display waiting for a customer to earn something from. A customer goes to the shopping mall to buy things he needs to live or be happy with. If we think about it, we shall realize that it was the love for what is desirable in this mortal world which brought them out of their homes, and in this silent process, gave the world a strong and ongoing social system. There is yet another element of wisdom behind it. If man had no liking for the blessings he finds in the mortal world, he would obviously have no taste or desire for blessings promised in the world to come. That being the case, why would he ever take the trouble of doing what is good and thus become deserving of Paradise, and not doing what is evil and thus become safe from Hell? There is still another element of wisdom which is more significant for consideration here. Is it not that man, with love for these things in his heart, has been put to a test as to who becomes engrossed in the enjoyments of the present life and forgets the life to come, and who comes to realize the real and temporal nature of these things, shows concern for them only in proportion to his needs, and then channels all his efforts into deeds that would make his next life good and safe? The wisdom behind the adornment of such things has been pointed out elsewhere in the Holy Qur'an: We made whatever there is on the earth its adornment so that We can test as to who among them acts best. The verse cited above clearly shows that the glamourizing of sue} desirable things is an act of God based on many wise considerations.

"Allah Himself is a Witness that there is no god worthy of worship except Him, and so are the angels and people of knowledge. He is the Maintainer of justice. There is no god worthy of worship except Him, the Almighty, All-Wise" The verse makes known that Allah bears witness that there is no god but Him, and that the angels and the people of knowledge also bear witness to this. The Jalālayn reads the witnessing as the making clear by God to His creation that He is the one God. The Maʿārif commentary explains that the being and the attributes of Allah are shown by the manifestation of the creation, and that the Messengers and the Books sent by Allah all confirm this truth. The Ibn Kathīr commentary gives the sense that none has the right to be worshipped but He, the Almighty, the All-Wise. The Tazkirul commentary states that the God of the universe is the One and only God, and that He likes justice. The Tanwīr reads the verse as the making known of the divine oneness, given by Allah in these words, and it reads the witness of Allah as enough even if no one else bears witness. The Mukhtaṣar explains that Allah testifies that He alone is worthy of worship, and that the angels and the people of knowledge testify to it too. The Qushayrī commentary reads the verse as the witness that God gives to Himself, and it reads the praise as the proof of His oneness. The reader is asked to see the verse as the greatest of witnesses, the witness of God Himself, joined to the witness of the angels and of those with knowledge.

**Allah bears witness.**

God bears witness that is to say He has made it clear to His creation through proofs and signs that there is no god none that is truly worshipped in existence except Him He has borne witness to this and the angels have also borne witness to this by affirming it and those of knowledge from among the prophets and the believers through their conviction and in words; upholding constantly and uniquely maintaining His creations with justice qā’iman ‘upholding’ is in the accusative because it is a circumstantial qualifier and is governed by the import of the statement implied to be something like tafarrada ‘He alone is upholding…’; there is no god except Him He has repeated it for emphasis; the Mighty in His Kingdom the Wise in His actions. Then there are the Messengers and Books sent by Allah, all confirming. that truth.

**None has the right to be worshipped.**

None has the right to be worshipped but He, the Almighty, the All-Wise Truly, the religion with Allah is Islam. According to established knowledge, the universe seems to be a completely unitary system.

**Allah Himself is the witness.**

(Allah (Himself) is witness) even if no one else bears witness (that there is no God save Him. And the angels) do also bear witness to that (and the men of learning) and the prophets and the believers bear witness to that. The angels and people of knowledge also testify to this, by declaring and calling to His Oneness.

**The witness of Allah to Himself.**

He Himself praised Himself and He Him self gave witness to Himself concerning His attributes as is worthy of Himself.

**What else the same passage holds.**

The subject of Tauhid (Oneness of Allah) which began with the opening of Surah 'Al- Imran reappears in the first verse in a very special manner. Allah bears witness that none has the right to be worshipped but He, and the angels, and those having knowledge (also bear witness to this); (He always) maintains His creation in justice. Out of the three witnesses mentioned here, the evidence of Allah Almighty is in a figurative sense. It means that the being and the attributes of Allah and the manifestations of His power and creativity all over are open signs of His Oneness. Those who were given the Scripture (Jews and Christians) did not differ except out of rivalry, after knowledge had come to them. And whoever disbelieves in the Ayat of Allah, then surely, Allah is Swift in reckoning So if they dispute with you say: The second testimony mentioned is that of angels who are close to Allah. "I have submitted myself to Allah, and (so have) those who follow me. They carry out His instructions and bear testimony (knowing and seeing) that Allah alone is worthy of worship. " And say to those who were given the Scripture (Jews and Christians) and to those who are illiterate (Arab pagans): The third witness is that of the men of knowledge. This expression, ulul ilm, means the blessed prophets and men who have the knowledge of Islam. Imam al-Ghazali and Ibn Kathir find this a matter of great honour for Ulama for Allah has mentioned their witness along with His, and that of angels. It is also possible that the term, ulul ilm (the men of knowledge) may, in an absolute sense, be referring to those who, by conducting an inquiry based on sound intellectual principles, or by deliberating into this universe, could acquire the knowl-edge of the unity of Allah Almighty - even if they are not alim or 'men of knowledge' in the traditional sense, whose knowledge is acquired under a formal discipline from Islam's own original sources. The next verse clearly settles that the only faith' ( din) acceptable to Allah is Islam. Thus, totally excluding any other faith or religion as acceptable to Allah, the verse completes the subject of Allah's Oneness, any opposition to which is doomed. Merits of the verse meaning "Allah bears witness" The verse beginning with : 'shahidal-lahhu' has a special elegance. Imam al-Baghawi the renowned mufassir reports that two leading Jewish scholars came to Madīnah from Syria. With the township of Madīnah before them, they started talking to each other about the looks of the place which matched the prophecy in Torah that the last of the prophets would be living here. Later, they came to know that someone very pious lives here and whom people refer to as the prophet. They went to see the Holy Prophet sight of him reminded them of all attributes which Torah had predicted he would have. They presented themselves before him and said: If you answer it correctly, we shall embrace Islam. "Which is the greatest witness in the Book of Allah? " This verse of 'shahadah' (witness) was revealed as an answer to this question. According to a hadith in the Musnad of Ahmad, when the Holy Prophet recited this verse in Arafat, he said right after that: Whoever recites this verse and then says: ; (And to that, 0 my Lord, I too am a witness), Allah Almighty will say to the angels on the Last Day: 'My servant has made a promise while I am the Foremost to keep a promise when I make it, so let my servant be admitted into Paradise.' (Ibn Kathir) Another hadith from Sayyidna Abu Ayyub al-Ansari narrates that the Holy Prophet said: 'Whoever recites Ayah al-Kursi (2:255) and the Ayah : Qulil-lahumma malik al-mulki upto ‌ bighairi hisab (3:26, 27), Allah Almighty will forgive all his sins, admit him to Paradise and take care of seventy (i.e. plenty) of his needs, the simplest of these being his forgiveness.' (Ruh a1-Ma ani with reference to Dailami)

The Jalālayn reads the religion pleasing to God as the submission of the self to Him, and it reads the Scripture as the book given to the Jews and the Christians, who differed over it. The Maʿārif commentary explains that in this meaning those who believed in the prophets and the messengers before the Prophet are also the ones who submitted, and it reads the meaning of the word Islam as particular to the religion of the Prophet. The Qushayrī commentary reads the authority of the living over the dead as the sign of the Lord who is able to do all things. **The night and the day.**

If we were to take 'the living' and the dead' in a broad and general sense, this will become inclusive of the learned and the ignorant, the perfect and the imperfect and the believer and the disbeliever (the Muslim and the Kafir).

**You give power to whom You will.**

Verily, You are able to do all things You make the night to enter into the day, and You make the day to enter into the night, You bring the living out of the dead, and You bring the dead out of the living. He brings into existence life from dead elements and causes living things to die.

You bring out the living from the dead – as in a believer from a disbeliever and crops from seed – and You bring out the dead from the living – as in a disbeliever from a believer and a chick from an egg.

You make the night pass into the day such that the authority of the light of unity tawḥīd prevails and nothing remains of the traces of the lower self and its darknesses.
